newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary MKB expands, sees above-target 1996 results.
newsitem.headline: Hungary MKB expands, sees above-target 1996 results.

text.p: Hungary's second largest commercial bank, Magyar Kulkereskedelmi Bank (MKB) on Monday reported continued expansion in the first half and said it hoped for above-target 1996 results.

"During the first half of 1996, MKB continued its vigorous business expansion targeted simultaneously at an offensive market share acquisition and the ongoing enhancement of earning capacity," MKB said in a statement.
"This year will be fairly successful for MKB," General Director Tamas Erdei told a news conference.
MKB, which is majority-owned by Germany's Bayerische Landesbank, increased its pre-tax profits to 4.265 billion forints in the first six months from 3.196 billion in the corresponding period of 1995.
MKB's assets amounted to 277 billion forints on June 30, down from 331 billion at the end of last year, mainly because MKB repaid a large $350 million 20-year loan 10 years ahead of maturity.

This was possible because of a $3 billion privatisation revenue of last year which helped Hungary to reduce its state debt, Erdei said. MKB was a mediator to the National Bank of Hungary (NBH) in the U.S. zero bond deal.
However, MKB's assets, not including the $350 million loan, increased by 31 percent in the first half of this year from the same period of last year, Erdei said.
In June MKB held 7.7 percent of corporate deposits in Hungary, up from 7.2 percent in 1995.

It also boosted its market share in corporate loans with less then one year maturity to 9.7 percent from 7.5 percent. MKB's market share in corporate foreign currency lending was over 16 percent in June.
MKB said it planned to increase the number of its branches to 19 from 12 this year and was in advanced negotiations to acquire a stake in an unnamed foreign bank.

Erdei said MKB planned to become a key regional bank in Central and Eastern Europe and he saw the growing economies north of Hungary, as well as Croatia and Slovenia, as potential fields of expansion for his bank.

Erdei added MKB expected better results this year than in 1995 despite declining interest rates and narrowing margins on the Hungarian market, where all banks will have to face sharper competition in the next two years.

He said MKB planned to increase its presence in financing the energy sector, which Hungary has almost fully privatised and where the new Western investors are likely to invest hundreds of billion forints in modernisation in the next few years.
